newsitem.title: CHINA: China mulls overseas bond issues for state firms.
newsitem.headline: China mulls overseas bond issues for state firms.

text.p: China said on Wednesday it was considering allowing large state-owned companies to issue bonds on foreign markets but analysts said there have been no concrete signs Beijing would let firms make issues in the near future.
"The state... will gradually give state firms the right to issue foreign bonds," the China Daily newspaper said.
China now permits only 13 financial institutions to issue bonds abroad but some of the funds raised had been used by key firms and in vital projects, the newspaper said.

"As state firms speed up their reform to build a modern corporate system, conditions for allowing them to go directly to the international market are maturing," the newspaper said, but gave no timetable.
Chinese officials reached by telephone declined to comment, and analysts said Beijing had not indicated when it would allow firms to make issues.
"There's been nothing," said one foreign analyst in Shanghai.
But analysts said many large Chinese firms would have to eventually turn to overseas bond markets to fund long-term investments which mature in 10-20 years.
"It has been talked about and I think there may be more intense discussion," said one Hong Kong-based analyst. "China does not have the domestic markets that have those long maturities."
Overseas issues would be inevitable as China continued its drive to push through market-oriented reforms and create a more open economy, analysts said.
"The government is moving towards more capital account liberalisation and that means they're thinking about letting other entities go abroad," the analyst said.
China could well afford corporate issues abroad because it had a strong external debt service capacity, its coffers stuffed with more than $110 billion in foreign exchange, he said.
"They can feel marginally more relaxed by having a few more borrowers out there in the market provided that it makes sense from those companies' overall funding strategies," he said.
Beijing's tight credit policy meant many firms were unable to obtain funds needed to fuel expansion plans or service their working capital requirements, another Hong Kong analyst said.

The commercialisation of China's banks, although moving at a snail's pace, had nonetheless made banks more choosy in lending their money, thus further tightening credit for companies, the second analyst said.
"These organisations have been stunted in their ability to expand," he said.
The most likely candidates for overseas bond issues would be large industrial groups that had already listed shares in Hong Kong or New York, the analysts said.
Firms that had listings abroad would be armed with better accounting procedures as well as the degree of openness needed to attract foreign capital, the first analyst said.
Beijing would likely first give the go-ahead to firms involved in pricey sectors such as infrastructure, utilities, heavy industry, power, fertiliser or petrochemicals, the second analyst said.
"You're looking for a company with a significantly large funding requirement that it makes sense to tap global markets," he said.
